source.title: BiomechGPT: Extending Motion-Language Models to Clinical Motion Understanding
source.authors: Rui-Ze Yang; Ann Kennedy; R. J. Cotton

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether downstream performance improves with model and training-data scale in a motion-language setting, but uses clinical task scores rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The study cites language-model scaling work and reports its own model- and dataset-size sweeps on downstream clinical motion tasks. It does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws, test extrapolation from smaller runs, or identify compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.test_reason: The study reports downstream clinical motion-task scores across fine-tuned Gemma backbones (1B, 4B, 12B) and fine-tuning data sizes. That bears on V6, only coarsely, in a new setting (QLoRA fine-tuning on motion tokens). It measures no pretraining loss and fits no scaling curve, so it is T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that aggregate clinical-task performance rises with backbone size and training data, while effects vary by task. They add that the data benefit is largest at small model sizes.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes instruction-tuned Gemma-family backbones with QLoRA on motion-token question-answer tasks and evaluates downstream clinical metrics. It does not use the original studies' held-out text-pretraining-loss measurements or fit their scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies across task; dataset composition and test-set source are varied. The authors report that aggregate gains from additional data are smaller at larger model sizes and that individual task scaling effects vary.
record.problems: The study measures downstream scores rather than held-out pretraining loss and does not fit power laws or evaluate extrapolation. Aggregate scores hide task-level variation; several individual scores decrease with added data. Results are averaged across three repeats, but uncertainty intervals for the scaling table values are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: The per-task scaling tables and Figure 5 report many additional task-by-model values. The aggregate results and three explicit individual-task decreases are retained; the remaining per-task cells are omitted because they do not alter the reported aggregate trend or add a distinct condition-level conclusion. Tokenizer reconstruction and tokenizer-choice ablations are omitted because they do not test scaling performance.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute; power-law form.
Extrapolation of fitted laws from small to large runs.
Effect of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Whether a power-law form holds for motion or fine-tuning. Only three backbone sizes are used, with no fitted law and no loss curves.
Quantitative predictability: no curve fit and no prediction of held-out sizes. No link to pretraining loss. No sizes beyond 12B. Only three sizes and three data levels.
Dependence of exponents or optimal splits on setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: Per-task decreases with model size: TUG 1B 0.8154 vs 4B 0.7626, FSST 1B 0.7624 vs 4B 0.6833, and fall history Med4B below 4B. These show non-monotonic task-level scaling.
Two-task versus ten-task results: the 12B two-task sum without HumanML3D (1.7707 in the 10-task set) is below 4B and Med4B. Three-way ANOVA gives model size p<0.001.
Model-size by data interaction: the benefit of added data shrinks at larger sizes, and 1B+HumanML3D beats 4B and Med4B without it.

record.verdict_notes: This is a scaling-of-fine-tuned-backbones result with only three Gemma sizes plus a same-size medical variant. It gives weak, qualitative evidence for V6 and none for power-law forms. Data scaling here means fine-tuning data, partly from a different source (HumanML3D), not pretraining tokens. The 4B data sweep is evaluated on the multi-camera test set only. Values are means of three repeats, and no intervals are given in the tables.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in motion or other modalities, or in fine-tuning; the study measures downstream task performance, not power-law loss.
The study tests downstream clinical motion-task performance against model and dataset scale, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a quantitative scaling curve.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices, and bending of power-law curves.

relationships.condition: Aggregate 10-task score versus Gemma-3 backbone size (1B/4B/12B) and versus fine-tuning data level for the 4B model
relationships.reason: Aggregate sums rise monotonically with backbone size (r1,r3,r7; r2,r4,r8). The 4B data sweep also rises (r9-r11). ANOVA p=0.003 for model size and p=0.007 for data level.
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate scores rise monotonically with backbone size and increase with fine-tuning data for the 4B model, with ANOVA p = 0.003 for size and p = 0.007 for data level.

relationships.condition: Individual clinical tasks, and the size effect when HumanML3D data is added
relationships.reason: Adding data lowers several individual task scores (r12-r14). Per-task size trends are non-monotonic (Table 5, not in rows). With added data the 1B to 4B aggregate gain is nearly flat (r2 vs r4), so gains are not uniformly predictable.
relationships.display_finding: Adding HumanML3D data lowered several task scores, individual size trends were non-monotonic, and aggregate improvement from 1B to 4B became nearly flat.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
